utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague, my Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman and I appear with Cynthia McMurrey for Mr. Esad Landzo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Kindly bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you can proceed. WITNESS R (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Good morning, Mr. R.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I trust you had a quiet and restful evening and that you are refreshed and ready to go forward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, having seen Kusterica's film on the disintegration of a country, "There once was a country".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you watched a film last night about Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the dissolution of Yugoslavia from the standpoint of the film director Kusterica, as he saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to return the exhibit we were using at the close of testimony yesterday back to the ELMO, please. Mr. R, I would like you to just look at the document that has been placed on the ELMO and verify for the record that it was the same drawing we were discussing at the close of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go back a bit and do a bit of clarification with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back a bit and do a little clarification with regard to this drawing. You drew this yourself, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 19th October 1995, you had a meeting with Mr. Regis Abribat, an investigator from the OTP, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know the exact date, but I said it was either October or November 1995, I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whatever that date was, it was on that date that you gave him this drawing that you had made of the Celebici camp, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after I made the statement, the investigator asked if I could make a drawing of Celebici itself, and on the basis of my recollection, I made the drawing. Of course some things differ from reality and from the model, but that is how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you at that time set out to deliberately make that drawing inaccurate, to try to fool Mr. Abribat or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Therefore I take it that you did not tell Mr. Abribat at that time that you had not done a good job and that this was an inaccurate drawing and that he should not rely on it; you did not tell him anything like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not tell him, but let me repeat, the statement made under -- those circumstances differ considerably from the circumstances we are talking under today, when Mr. Abribat asked me about the manholes where people were put and suffocated and put in water. I roughly indicated it, but, as I have already said, throughout my stay in the Celebici camp I was never taken to those manholes, nor did I pass by them, so I did not go to that spot where the pump station was, the petrol station was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, you intended that Mr. Abribat leave that meeting understanding and believing that you had made as accurate a drawing as your memory would permit at that point; is that not fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that the court would take measures and find ways to make a true model. What I drew differs from the model, so this should be attributed to my own bad recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am going to ask you the question again and ask you to listen very carefully and see if you can answer the question that I ask. You intended for Mr. Abribat to leave that meeting believing that you had given him as accurate a drawing as your memory at that time would permit; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Going back to this drawing, I would like you to look where on the drawing you have placed building number 22. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that the model sitting in front of you is inaccurate with the place where it places building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the model is quite accurate. It is the drawing that is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you again about the gas station, and understand that I am asking you about the gas station, not about any manholes. I have not asked you any questions about manholes and do not intend to. You told us yesterday that the gas station is improperly placed on your drawing because you really did not have any opportunity to see that gas station, that you just basically heard about it from others; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday that when you were in hangar number 6 that you were frequently taken out or allowed to go out to a latrine behind hangar number 6, early in your experience with four or five other people and then in the larger groups at a later time. That is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that was a misinterpretation because I did not say I went out frequently, but very rarely. If I spent 99 days in the camp and mentioned two or three times going out, I do not think one can describe it as being frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought you had told us that there was a daily routine where groups of you were taken out and given a certain amount of time to use the latrine and then brought back in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the groups are concerned. I said it happened twice a day, in the morning about 7, 8 or 9, depending on when Mr. Delic arrived, and in the afternoon; twice during the day, 40 seconds each time. I do not know whether that is frequent or infrequent, twice a day, 40 seconds each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But before those larger groups, you went out in smaller groups and had more time to spend at the latrine, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at the beginning, as I said, maybe in the month of June. Later on, all that was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many days it was that you were in hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent somewhere from the beginning of June, as I said yesterday, that was one week after my arrest, and that was on 26th May, so that could have been the beginning of June, until 31st August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So roughly three months, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, June, July and August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is roughly 90 days, give or take a few days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Plus the time spent in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am only talking about hangar 6 now. My question is directed to the time you were there, and it was roughly 90 days then that you were confined in hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you went out to that latrine two times a day, then over a 90 day period you would have been out at that latrine perhaps 180 times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "there"? What area are you referring to when you say "there"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was talking about the latrine area behind hangar number 6. If you went out there twice a day for 90 days, that would mean you went to that latrine at least 180 times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me repeat again what I have already said. If necessary, I can show you on the model where we went to relieve ourselves. As I said yesterday, according to a procedure that was established and invented by Mr. Delic, there would be 50 of us standing in line to urinate and Mr. Delic was walking behind us all the time, flourishing a baseball bat, and we were waiting to get a blow rather than to do our business. I do not know how I could look around to see where is the pump, where is the hangar where the other people are, all this in 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will ask you the question again. I thought we had made an agreement yesterday that you would listen to my question and attempt to answer it. The only question that I asked you was, if you were in that hangar 90 days and went out to the latrine twice a day, you probably went out to that latrine about 180 times; do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How is it that in 180 times standing out there at that latrine you failed to notice that rather large gas station right across the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you think we were free to look around to see where things where, where people were? As I said, we were in line with our heads bowed, without the right to turn around. There was Mr. Delic behind us, who was always there with a baseball bat in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you were never free to look around and get any idea of what the camp looked like, why did you make a drawing for Mr. Abribat of what the camp looked like? Why did you not just tell Mr. Abribat you had no idea because you could not ever look around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I tried as far as was possible in answer to the gentleman's question, I do not remember his name, the investigator's question, to give some kind of a rough outline of the camp where we were detained. As you see from the drawing itself, the position of building number 6 and the machine-gun nests were accurately drawn. Those were the things that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you will look at that drawing, you will notice that a number of notations on there are written in English. Is that your writing or someone else's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you read and write English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that important for the investigation in this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The way it works here is I ask the questions and you give the answers. My question is: do you read and write English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point in time, yes; until the beginning of the war, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, if you will look at your drawing, on the right-hand side, near what would be the entrance to the camp, you have drawn a couple of buildings up above the road; do you see the buildings I am referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did the person who made this model in front of you fail to include those buildings in the model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Having told us that this drawing was your best recollection at the time of the layout of the camp, how is it you are able today to tell us that the model sitting in front of you is accurate? How do you know that it is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the model is in three dimensions and it gives a much better portrayal of the real situation than an ordinary drawing. This three dimensional model somehow refreshes one's memory regarding details forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it is your position that when you saw the model it refreshed your memory and you remembered that the model is correct and your drawing is wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you that this model was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw the model for the first time when I sat at this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess what I am wondering is if your best memory of Celebici camp is what was reflected in your drawing, how on earth can you tell us with that same memory that the model in front of you is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I object to Defence lawyer's continuing on this line of questions. The question was asked and answered already. The witness said already that the drawing he did on request of the OTP was imprecise and I think there is nothing else he might answer on this line of questions. I think going on in this line of questions might turn out to be harassment of the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you were merely asking his opinion, you are asking the opinion of the witness. If he gives you his opinion you might accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the question I asked you or would you like to hear it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please ask it again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not going to be able to give you the same words, but I will do the best I can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Back in October 1995 when you drew this map for Mr. Abribat, it was your best memory of the way the camp looked, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the statement itself was given within a short period of time. The gentleman did not have much time at his disposal, nor did I , for that matter, because I was working. It was all done in haste without giving it any detailed thought, it was done the way it was and it was done inaccurately, so let me repeat for the fifth time that the model is accurate, that the drawing is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. If Mr. Abribat had returned to The Hague and built a nice three dimensional model like the one you see in front of you based upon the drawing you gave him, then I suspect when you saw it you would have told us that was an accurate model; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to these hypothetical questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has told you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am going to withdraw the question, your Honour. It is not necessary. You see some writing up in the left-hand corner of your drawing; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, though the photocopy is not very clear, so I cannot exactly see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word is probably, "handed in to Regis Abribat, investigator of the International Tribunal in The Hague for war criminals committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then that would be your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, please, sir. Where do you see my signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not sure I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There is no signature, otherwise we would not allow it to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says "Yugoslavia", what I thought was your signature is apparently "Yugoslavia". I want to talk to you about something else now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were telling us yesterday about the food that you received in hangar number 6, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that among the foods that you received, you got soup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that occasionally, very rarely, we did get soup as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you told us about that soup was that when you got it, it was two or three days old.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What special skills or powers do you have that enable you to judge the age of soup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very simple power; if you ate that soup and it was a little sour we would get diarrhoea and we could not go out, because Mr. Delic and the other guards would not let us go out, so that is a very simple method to conclude how the soup is old. It is a very simple method.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How does that method get you to the precision of two or three days? Why could it not be a week or one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been a week, why not. In any case, it was not soup that was fit for eating. For soup that produces diarrhoea, does it matter whether it is two days old or a week old, especially if you are not given any medical treatment afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it really does not matter, except when you tell this court, this Tribunal, that the soup was two or three days old yesterday and then tell us today that it could have been a week old, what that indicates to this Tribunal is you are just guessing about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, you asked me what my visionary abilities were to tell how old the soup was. I am not a visionary. If I had been a visionary, I would not have ended up in the camp, I would have been somewhere else if I had known what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you also told us yesterday that, as a general rule, the only food that you would get beyond some occasional soup was five grammes of bread a day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never mentioned five grammes, I just, as far as I remember -- again, to use the same sentence that you used, I will not be able to repeat what I said in the same words -- I said that the bread was made from mouldy flour, so it had a very unpleasant taste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. You remember the question that I just asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me whether I remembered that I said we were given five grammes of bread. I did not say five grammes, so allow me to repeat what I said. It was made from very -- please allow me to finish the answer to your question. Be kind enough to hear me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was it that I asked you what the bread was made out of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did not ask me that, but you asked me whether it was correct that I had said that we received five grammes of bread, and I never mentioned yesterday five grammes. I just said that the loaf was divided up into 14, 15, 16, 18 pieces. I never mentioned five grammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you did tell us yesterday about the quality of that bread, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did yesterday, I started again today and you interrupted me, so I do not know whether you are asking me questions and not allowing me to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you feel a need to repeat the quality of that bread today even though not asked about it because you believe that those of us sitting here in the courtroom are not capable of hearing what you are saying and understanding it and that you need to say it over and over?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object to this arguing between the Defence lawyer and the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is cross-examination, this is not arguing. One judge once told me on cross-examination you are supposed to argue with the witness. I think it was an appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If the argument is in the nature of a question, then it is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please repeat your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was: do you think those of us here are incapable of hearing and understanding what you are saying so that you have to repeat it over and over, even if not asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you arrived here in The Hague for the purpose of appearing before this Tribunal, could you tell us with whom you have discussed your memory of what happened at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I discussed it with Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Turone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How much time did you spend discussing it with Mr. Turone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was four and a half to five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What day would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was last Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you had any further discussions with Mr. Turone about these matters since that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we continued the following day on Monday, but I am not sure for how long. It was short.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about yesterday evening, did you have any discussions with Mr. Turone yesterday evening about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not only did I not discuss it with Mr. Turone, but with no one. I just told you how I spent my evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about this morning? Did you have any discussion with Mr. Turone this morning about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I see Mr. Turone for the first time now as I sat down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about with Witness J? Did you have discussions with Witness J about your experiences in Celebici since you have been here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How is it that you know who Witness J is if you had not had a discussion with him about his testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I know that there was only one other person who was here during my stay, and I know his identity, I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please do not say who he is, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You certainly had meetings with Witness J during the time he was here in The Hague and you were here in The Hague, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went to dinner together. However, the ladies, that is the staff that is taking care of the security arrangements here, they prevented us from discussing anything relating to the trial and what we discussed was potential business, so our discussions did not relate to the testimony or The Hague. And I have to add that the staff would always stop conversation, saying that this could harm the whole procedure or the whole trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if they had to stop conversation, it means there was some going on for them to stop, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would not start, but we would have -- they did it as an introductory remark, not to discuss issues relating to the trial, things that were going on in the courtroom, so this was a warning of sorts, or a caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we might all be somewhat baffled by your statement that they would stop you and say you should not be discussing these matters and then tell us you were not discussing these matters. There would be no occasion for them to stop you if you never had such discussion, would there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the way you phrase your question is contradictory in itself. As I said, when we sat down to dinner, we would be told, "please do not discuss matters that transpired in the courtroom today", so we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess you are telling us they were with you at dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were they with you at breakfast yesterday morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at breakfast, lunch and dinner, if I need to say that, and the entire way from the hotel room to the, whatever I should call it, the dining area or the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any time you had occasion to be with Witness J then these persons were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you take very seriously this appearance before the International Tribunal and your testimony here, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How to answer this question? I do not know how you want me to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not see it as a situation of great fun and merriment and a situation in which it is irrelevant whether your testimony is accurate or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am also not sure about this question. Can you clarify it for me, please? Can you simplify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sure. You want your testimony before this International Tribunal to be as accurate as you can make it, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You agreed with me yesterday that your memory of the events of Celebici was better as one goes back in time, so that fairly immediately after it your memory would have been better than it would be now, five years later, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that that is a normal process, that people forget, but I also said that some events like deaths and beatings, the mistreatments that we were subjected to, have a strong impact, they are significant and those images of death remain there forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There have been occasions in the past, have there not, when your memory of events was committed to writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Being both an intelligent man and a man who is interested in giving accurate testimony before this Tribunal, you carefully reviewed all those prior written representations of your memory of Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the first part of your statement is, regarding my intelligence, I would not like to comment on that, but as far as the second part, my answer is yes, with the solemn declaration in front of me, and as far as the third part, I did give written statements. I just want to add regarding this third part and you said that yourself, you cannot repeat the same phrase the same way. If I were able to do that, I would be a computer, not a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think my question was probably hopelessly confusing, let me try it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave you a three part answer, so if you want to simplify the question, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is my intent. The major issue I am interested in is, you carefully reviewed all these prior written representations of your memory so that you could be as accurate as possible in front of this Tribunal, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in The Hague, this was fairly superficial, it took about ten minutes. However, I have given multiple statements and maybe they differ based on what the investigators or the people who were asking questions were emphasising, what they wanted to focus on. So it depends on the occasion, whether it was literary or investigative, or whether it was depending on what methods were used for torture or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it your position that you have not carefully reviewed prior written statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not carefully, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Understanding that your prior memory may have been more accurate, you did not think it was important to refresh today's memory with that more accurate memory of the past?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the question is a bit equivocal. Can you phrase it in simpler terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First you have told us that your memory was better as we go back in time, and that that memory has been recorded in statements, and then you have told us that in preparation to give accurate testimony to this Tribunal, you did not bother to carefully review those statements. I believe that is your position; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, the majority of these statements, with the exception of one that I have given to Mr. Regis, were not given for The Hague Tribunal, they were given on different occasions, and at different times, and it is possible that in some parts, they differ from one another. It is probable and it is normal that they should differ, and it is dependent on the purpose of it being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So did you deliberately put inaccuracies in those statements prior to the one you gave the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Never been asked, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: About statements, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has never answered, that I hear, deliberately giving wrong answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have never asked it and he has never answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can answer it. Did you deliberately give wrong answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir, restate your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the statements you did prior to the OTP statement, did you deliberately give wrong information in those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Could I please ask how you qualify this deliberate wrong testimony, because they were never testimonies, they were not statements given in court, they were given to different either committees or bodies that were collecting evidence or documentation on Celebici and, as I said, it is impossible to give the same exact statement twice. Then we would be machines who repeat the same thing. Then you could just make one recording of it and replay it, you need not have witnesses testifying then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just told us you had never given a statement to a court before, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, this is my first testimony before a Tribunal, any Tribunal in any country at any time, because my whole life in fact I tried not to be involved in anything that would bring me in conflict with law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you not on 2nd March 1994 give a statement to an investigating judge of the District Court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, but that was not a trial, this was questioning for their own needs so this was just a meeting with a judge and conversation, similar to what occurred with Mr. Regis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So because this was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In other words, this was not a trial, it was gathering of information, and if you consider the statement I gave to Mr. Regis part of a trial, then that other statement was that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So since this statement to the District Court in Belgrade was not a trial, you did not feel any necessity of making your statement accurate, is that what you are trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I want to say is not only was it -- it was not a trial, this was gathering of information, collection of evidence. If what I had given to Mr. Regis was a trial, then that too was a trial; in other words there was a judge who was gathering evidence, and as I said, I have given different statements at different times for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You have not answered the question so let me ask it again. Because the statement you made to the District Court in Belgrade was not a trial, did you feel that you had no obligation to tell the truth or to be accurate in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely said the truth and I was accurate as much as I could be and I was answering the questions asked of me by the judge, which considered legal matters from his point of view on what happened in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were answering those questions to the best of your memory at that time, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sure you will agree with me that when we write down things we want to remember it is very helpful to go back and review them, to refresh our memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many written statements have you given regarding your experiences in Celebici? How many times have accounts that you have given been reduced to writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell exactly, but I think you may have all these statements in front of you and you can compare them. I do not know how many times. There were various occasions at different times, different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just do that then. I have in my possession a statement dated 18th February 1993, given to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre; do you remember that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I stated, I remember some of the statements, that is most of the places and most of the statements. Now what is contained within each individual statement is dependent on what people were interested in, the political aspects, the number of victims, the number of murders, even literary aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You must think that we are incapable of hearing and understanding your answers because you keep giving the same ones over and over. Let me ask the question again. On 18th February 1993 -- I have a statement that you gave to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre; do you remember giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that the first statement that you recall giving regarding your experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it was the first but since you have all the statements, you can compare them and see if it was the first. I really do not know if it was the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question, "why did I make the statement". How do you mean, "why did I give the statement"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did someone ask you to do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was asked and I accepted it gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was that asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where were you, did somebody call you or did somebody come to where you were? How did it happen that you were called upon to make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the circumstances prior to the giving of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your memory of what happened four years ago is rather poor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not consider the giving of the statement very significant and so I did not consider it a very important thing and so my memory of it is not very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you have given so many statements you cannot remember today how many you have given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not that many statements, but there were multiple statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, you have them in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you believe that I have all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you do have, why not? They are no secret, they were made publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You believe you made more than five statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not answer that question, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you believe you made more than four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are repeating the same, five, four, three, six.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So as you sit there now, you just cannot remember how many statements you have given, is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, asked and answered many times already, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe it has been. If I were to tell you that I have in front of me six statements, would you then agree that you have given six statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this question was already answered and that I answered it. I do not know the exact number of answers, I would have to sit down and take a piece of paper and try to figure out when I have given all the statements. That would take a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object also to this way of questioning about the number of statements Mr. Ackerman might have in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the District Court in Belgrade on 2nd March 1994; you remember that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did you give that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave that statement because at that time there was talk that sooner or later there will be a trial for the murders in Celebici, either at national level or another one, and then I was invited to give a statement to the judge. I do not know his name, but I think you have it in front of you. This was also as gathering of material, not in the form of a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who requested that you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was requested of me by that court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the court contacted you and asked you to come and give a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back for just a moment to your statement to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre on 18th February 1993. Where did you go to make that statement, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the Serbian Counsel Information Centre is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the time you went there to make the statement, were there other detainees there who had also been asked to come and make statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were detainees from other camps, from -- not from Celebici. There were detainees from Mostar and I think from somewhere in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there were no other Celebici detainees at the time you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no, perhaps during the day or the previous days or the following days, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did not see anyone there that had been a Celebici detainee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was giving my statement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the time you were at the Serbian Counsel Information Centre, any time, the day you were there to give your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not precisely yet, your Honour. During any of the time that you were there giving your statement did you see any other Celebici detainee or talk with any other Celebici detainee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not talk to anyone. Whether any one of the detainees may have come in and passed by, I do not know. I do not remember seeing anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing Witness J there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us make sure who Witness J is so as to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please do not say the name. A little while ago when I was talking to you about the person you were having dinner and breakfast with you here, you knew that was Witness J; that is the person we are referring to. Was he there the same day you were to give a statement to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been that same day, but at that moment, I was the only one making a statement and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The day you went to the District Court in Belgrade, on 2nd March 1994, were there other Celebici detainees there at that time to also give statements that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also gave a statement that we have discussed a little bit to Mr. Regis Abribat of the Office of the Prosecutor on 19th October 1995; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How was it you happened to give that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certain people called me up by phone, saying that two gentlemen would be coming to that town, gentlemen who were collecting evidence for the trial in The Hague, and that I should come and make a statement as one of the detainees of the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that is how it came about and you did in fact give Mr. Regis Abribat a statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Abribat was careful to make certain that that statement was translated to you in Serbo-Croatian so there was no question about whether you understood what you were saying and believed what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go back to kind of where we began. In your review of -- I want to ask you a different question. I have now talked with you about three statements. Do you, as you sit here today, remember any other statements that you have given with regard to your Celebici experiences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember some statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those statements were and to whom they were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those statements were given on different occasions and to different commissions that were collecting different data; in the case of The Hague Tribunal, to Mr. Regis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You may have misunderstood my question. My question is: other than the three statements that I have discussed with you, where else did you make statements regarding your experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was saying, I cannot exactly recall the names of those organisations, because there were quite a number of them. Some were private, some were state and non-governmental that wanted to learn the truth or at least some of the facts regarding what had happened at the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let us see if you can remember one of them. Just tell me one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember a statement I made to the Serbian Information Centre or the Information Centre of the Serbian Assembly or SABOR. I do not recall the exact name of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be different from the one we have already talked about of 18th February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, let us try again. Tell me the name of one statement that you have given that we have not talked about today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the three that we have discussed today, can you tell me one time that you gave a statement to someone else and who that was. That is what I am trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You suggested in some of your prior answers that you may have given some statements for literary purposes. Does that help you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is better to put the question straight to him, what you want him to answer. This type of roving question does not get one anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you give any statements to anyone for literary purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to explain that, "for literary purposes". Could you clarify that a little bit? What do you mean when you say "a statement for literary purposes"? Could you simplify the question a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am basically quoting an answer you gave to an earlier question about the accuracy of your statements. You said they were given for different purposes, some of them literary. Let me ask you what you meant when you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were not statements, in the sense of any written texts. Those were rather conversations with people, literary people, men of letters, who wanted to hear about those experiences, and to have them in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us the name, please, of one of those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not even one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you even tell us the name of one of those people that you talked to, even one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he does not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Do you know if any of those people have written any papers or books or anything that contained things that you told them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I could not tell you anything definite about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any written or published works or anything like that that contained your name, your accounts of what went on in Celebici, any such thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am unable to recall just now of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked about an organisation you gave a statement to that you referred to as "SABOR"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. Whether it is the Serbian SABOR's Information Centre or the other way, I am not quite sure of the title of that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That institution is not located in Serbia, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does the name Strahinja Zivak mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man, before the war in Konjic, was either director or one of the executives of the post in Konjic, and I know that just before the war he was wounding in an accident, driven to Sarajevo, then the war broke out and Celebici occurred and what happened that Strahinja Zivak, I do not know, whether he survived or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you had your meetings with Mr. Turone with regard to your testimony before this Tribunal, he showed you and gave you an opportunity to review the three statements that we have talked about, the Serbian Counsel Information Centre, District Court Belgrade and OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said very superficially, and without entering into the details. When I asked whether I could use them to refresh my memory or to read them more carefully, but Mr. Turone said that was not necessary, that it is sufficient to present what one remembers and that that would be quite sufficient considering everything that had happened in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a short time, just before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hold any positions of authority with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Prior to mid May 1992, you, of course, were aware of the events that were going on around you in Bosnia and Croatia, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might say yes and no. I was aware and I was not aware. If I had been fully aware, I would not have got to Celebici, but I would have been in a territory far beyond the one where all this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew that there were attacks by Serbian forces on a number of villages in Bosnia prior to May 1992; you knew that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as one could learn from the media, television and radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The television and radio was what? Did you get television from Belgrade or television from Sarajevo? Where were you getting television from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, we were able to watch several programmes, and a third.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You watched the station from Belgrade, that was during that time under the control of Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know under whose control Television Belgrade was; nor do I know under whose control the various television stations are today, but we watch reports from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever get the impression, as you were watching the television from Belgrade, that you were being subjected to propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I remember the shots from Kupres, beheaded people, bodies torn apart. Why is that propaganda if people were killed, if people were murdered, unless you think that one type of people should get killed and another sort should not. I do not see why one could describe as propaganda the shots of dismembered human bodies. If it is a human body then whoever did it is a criminal, whatever side he belongs to, whatever race and whatever religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any notion as you sit there today how many Muslims were slaughtered by the Serbian forces during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object to the relevancy, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know and I do not think the majority of us here can know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the time in early 1992, were you in agreement with Mr. Milosevic's plan for a greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know anything about that plan, nor did I agree with it, nor do I agree with any forcible reshaping of anything that already existed, if it can done by agreement. I was naive enough to believe that this could be done by peaceful means, and naive enough to be arrested and taken to the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it from that answer that you think ethnic cleansing is not a good idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course it is not a good idea, and any problems that exist can be resolved at a negotiating table by agreement, if there is goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you acquired your M48 weapon in Bradina, did you know at that time that the possession of such a weapon was against the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but already on 12th May there was an attack on Bradina, so Bradina was not attacking anyone at the time. It would be stupid for Bradina to try to attack at least 40 Muslim villages in the surroundings which had at least as many inhabitants as Bradina each, so this was a mere attempt to protect what one might call one's very life and property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew at that time in May, talking basically mid May 1992, you knew at that time, did you not, that Sarajevo was being shelled and was under siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking for mid May?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that, because the electricity and the telephone lines were down already in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew prior to that time the shelling had started in Sarajevo and Sarajevo had been placed under siege. It was a fact that was known to you by mid May 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know there were roadblocks in April, but what happened later in May, we were cut off from the world in every respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also know that the main road, the main transportation artery from Sarajevo to Mostar and the Adriatic passed through Bradina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Including the railroad, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would have been of great assistance to the Serb forces who had Sarajevo under siege to be able to block that road and cut it off so that supplies could not reach Sarajevo; strategically that would have been a good idea militarily, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object to this question. The witness is not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is easy for him to say that he does not know, it is very easy. He can answer that question, I do not see -- you can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what to answer. What do I have to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew that Bradina being on that main thoroughfare between Sarajevo and the Adriatic, it would be a good place because of its tunnels to shut off access to Sarajevo and assist in the siege of Sarajevo, assist the Serbian forces in the siege of Sarajevo; you knew that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the strategic point of view, that would be normal, but if we are talking about blowing up the tunnel, I can tell you who did it and when, if you are interested in that. It was an interruption, a breaking off of communication between Bradina and the rest of the world. We would not mine ourselves and shut ourselves to the world. There were forces other than us who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: were you present so that you could observe the blowing up of the tunnels at Bradina? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Bradina when a gentleman came for some kind of pretended negotiations, Mr. Musinovic Miralem. He was sitting in Pero Mrkajic's cafe with some kind of representatives of the village. I was not with them at the table but I was in the cafe when they were discussing the possibility of a joint solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is: were you at the tunnels when they were blown up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You see when you tease, you have problems. Your questions are teasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only question was, was he was at the tunnels when they were blown up, that is the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is telling you how he got to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He is telling me how to make a watch, and I asked him what time it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, were you at the tunnels in Bradina when they were blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not at the tunnels, but I was at the cafe. But the explosion was so strong that the house on the Bradina side of the tunnel, Dordic's house, was left roofless and many other houses in Zukici, their roofs or windows were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It makes sense in view of what we have been discussing that it would have been important to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time to relieve the siege of Sarajevo, to keep that road from Sarajevo to the Adriatic open; would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, sir, what the government in Sarajevo wanted. I was not a member of any government in Sarajevo or outside it, and I do not know what which government wanted. I know what happened to me in Celebici and that is what I am talking about and not about any assumptions of a political or any other nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the battle for Bradina, I think you have told us that you were located at the railway station; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you told us yesterday was that in the area you were in, there was no exchange of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Virtually, no. Behind was the village of Zukici, and from that side, there was hardly any exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was exchange of gunfire in -- to some extent there and to a larger extent in other places, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, what do you mean an exchange of fire to some extent; could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you said just before I asked you that question that around Zukici there was very little exchange of gunfire; almost non-existent, I think may have been your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I still stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That means there was some exchange of gunfire there and the other question that I want you to answer is; are you suggesting by that there was a greater exchange of gunfire in other parts of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the direction of Repovci there was far more shooting, and also Bradina was shelled from Repovci with various shells and grenades which fell all over the village, especially the centre of the village where the cafes are, the school, the butcher's shop, the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that time, you were not a member of any organised military group, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no organised military group. What do you mean, do you mean an army? What is an "organised military group", so that I can answer your question with precision?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you in an organisation that had commanders that were giving you orders? Did you have uniforms, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of us had any uniforms, nor did we belong to any army. These were just village guards that existed virtually everywhere for the security and the protection of the inhabitants, so we did not have uniforms. None of us had uniforms of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to take you to that period of time immediately after you surrendered and were taken into custody in Bradina, and the first question I want to ask you about that is: fairly soon following that surrender, you were beaten by the soldiers who took you into custody, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what you have told us is that in the process of loading you on to a truck there was a gauntlet that you had to go through, soldiers on both sides, beating you with chains, boards, weapons and other things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were beaten pretty severely at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what is "severely" according to your judgement, so it is rather difficult to answer when you talk about severe beatings, or a serious beating. I cannot see that any beating is not serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am willing to accept whatever definition you had in mind of a severe beating when you spoke to us yesterday about severe beatings. At that occasion, when you were being loaded on to the truck, in the context of your definition of the term "severe", you were beaten severely, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If one faints from the blows, I assume then one can only call it a severe beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were bleeding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina, no. In Celebici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said in one of the statements that in the process of going through that gauntlet you were hit on the head and that you were bleeding from the head and you still have a mark on your head from that beating. Was that inaccurate, when you said that in one of your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the beating that provoked the injury under which I have a scar was in Celebici at the entrance in front of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that that is what you said yesterday. I am not asking you what you said yesterday, I am asking you if you said in one of your statements that at the time you were being loaded on the truck you were hit in the head and you were bleeding and that you still have a mark on your head from that blow. If you said that happened in one of your statements at the truck in Bradina, is it your position now that that was an inaccuracy in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what was written down in this statement. We all passed through the gauntlet, we all got beaten, behind our heads, we all got beaten and they said, "do not look around, do not mention names", and we were beaten with anything that could bring about an injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not know what is written down in the statement because you were not given a full and fair opportunity to review your statements; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I object to this way of questioning? If the Defence lawyer has some particular point of the statement which he considers in contradiction, he should more clearly formulate his question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The objection seems to be unrelated to my question. My question, your Honour, was: the reason you do not recall what you said in your statement was because you were not given a full and fair opportunity to review your statement, is that correct? I am not referring to any particular part of the statement, I am referring generally to his statements. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are asking him whether he could not recall it because he did not review his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think that is a fair question to anybody, "because you did not review the statement you cannot recall it".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The testimony he has given us up to this point, your Honour, is that he was not given an opportunity to fully review his statements by Mr. Turone, that he was told by Mr. Turone that that was not important, so I believe that is a fair question based upon his prior testimony in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If there is any problem about his statements you want to confront him with, ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, I will do that. Throughout your journey to Celebici in that truck, you were beaten throughout that journey also, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the drive to Celebici, but it was not on the road, it was on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those beatings were administered by the soldiers who had taken you into custody at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the instruments that was used to beat you during that journey was what I believe you have described as a "thick iron bar", correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a metal bar, I do not know if it was made of aluminium or steel, that I do not know, but it was a metal bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you suggest -- let me just ask you this: would you agree with me that you said in your statement to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre that that bar was a thick iron bar? Could you have said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether I said it was iron or metal but it was made of metal. Iron is also metal, based on my knowledge from the chemistry classes from school, so iron is also metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me read to you from your statement to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre, page 1: "One of the guards in the truck had a thick iron bar with which he beat us as we lay on the floor of the truck, one on top of the other. It was night-time and we did not know where they were taking us." That is the truth, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you finally arrived in Celebici, as you were getting out of the truck, you were knocked unconscious, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that point, two guards were taking one person after another and would hit each person in the back of the head, so when I fell down on this asphalt, I just heard something and I was semiconscious. If you had received a blow in the back of your head, you are dazed, semiconscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you were all lined up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, we had to take off our clothes except for our underwear, so if you had pants or jackets on or shoes, they paid special attention to the laces and belts and so all this was thrown on a heap in front of the tunnel. Then the beating against the wall ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you were lined up against the wall, you were beaten for some time by the soldiers then, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These were the same soldiers who had brought you there in the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say if it were the same soldiers who had brought us in the truck or the soldiers who were waiting for us. As I said, I was semiconscious, my hands were behind my head and they were giving orders, "do not look around, do not mention any names". Just one correction, we were not lined up all against the wall. One would be thrown off the truck and then beaten and then taken into the tunnel, not all of us lined up one next to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So for you personally, I know you have told us that and said that those beatings along that wall lasted for five or six hours that night, you personally, when you were put against that wall, for how long a period were you beaten there by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a personal or subjective perception, if you are standing against a wall half naked and people around you are kicking you with their boots, with all kinds of objects, your estimation of time is very subjective category.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will accept that. By the time you were finally put into tunnel number 9, you had had several ribs broken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had a cut on top of your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had a broken nose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had lost consciousness many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you were put in tunnel 9 and throughout the period of time you were in tunnel 9, you were not beaten during that period of time before being moved to hangar 6, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, personally I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you got to hangar number 6 and during the whole period of time you were in hangar number 6, you were only beaten two or three times, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, twice personally before the last time after the visit of the Red Cross, so altogether three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of an organisation called the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. R. That is all I have. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honours, it is my turn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. R.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you tired already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite a bit, because if I can say, to keep in mind all this information and all those ugly details, it is exhausting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, I think we will have a respite and break for now and come back after lunch at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Registry has informed me that the exhibit that I used during the long first part of my cross-examination was not tendered by me and I would like to do that now, the drawing of Celebici camp that was done by Witness R, and so I would therefore like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I hope you are refreshed now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Olujic, you may continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. R, once again, my name is Zeljko Olujic, I represent Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Before I put a number of questions to you, I should like to say something that my learned colleague who questioned you before me did not mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, we have a technical problem here, Ms McMurrey is not getting any translation, for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly get the technicians to see to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
