utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth? Can the counsel hear now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue now. I think everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. R, I wanted to point out that my learned colleague, who talked to you a moment ago, was speaking in English, and there was time for you, until the translation was completed, for you to think and to answer the question, but there was no real opportunity for a proper dialogue, and such a risk does exist between you and me because I am speaking Croatian and you are speaking Serbian. It is a language that we can both understand so that to avoid a dialogue between us we have to wait for my question to be translated, so that I shall slow down, and I would also like you to wait for my question to be translated before you give your answer. Have we understood each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. R, as an intellectual, you were able to fully gain insight into the events that developed in the spring of 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me remind the witness, wait for the interpretation to be concluded before you answer, because we too are following. We do not understand two of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. R.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer may be ambiguous, both yes and no, in the sense that the country had already been swept by the flame of the war and on the other hand no, because if I had been wise enough, I would not have got to the camp in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, have you served in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I did my military service in the JNA; if you need the year I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, that is all I needed to know. Mr. R, did you acquire any rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the rank of a leader of a group, like any other soldier, squad leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you did acquire rank, the lowest rank, but it is a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the rank of a soldier, not an officer rank. It is the lowest rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During your military service, did you receive an Award of Merit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was an honour in 1978/79: it also meant 15 days less of service, as you are well aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that I did not do my military service --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Which branch of the military did you serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Since you were an exemplary soldier with the lowest rank, which is not an officer rank, in the camp in Celebici, did the behaviour of the guards there remind you of the behaviour of troops, of military men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the morning, you the prisoners, the detainees, were you expected to appear at a review?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did the guards have a review of troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they did in the command building, that was beyond my vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: As far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. They may have had it in the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was there a review of troops at dusk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was the military music played at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were people in the camp wearing one uniform or several uniforms; in other words, were there different units present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that at the beginning there were different uniforms, but later on those uniforms became the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the so-called MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who the MUP people were, nor what was the difference between the MUP members, the Green Berets, or whatever they were called, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But there were some at the beginning, as far as you know, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: While you were in the camp, did the guards sometimes waste ammunition for no purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you know, of course, whether you ever heard any one of the guards being called to task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, I just know, as I mentioned yesterday, Mr. Murici, who was an Albanian and who treated us quite humanely for a couple of days, he was removed very soon and this applied to other guards who showed any understanding for the detainees or any compassion. They would be very shortly after that removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: While you were in the camp, Mr. R, did you ever witness any refusal by the guards to carry out orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I have a moment to think? Yes, I remember once there was such a case in the hangar itself. I only know what I saw with my own eyes within the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Of course. Again, I am asking you to answer to the best of your knowledge; were there any conflicts among the guards at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that in Celebici. There were other conflicts in Konjic, but we are not talking about those now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me please, you are a protected witness, but my question does not affect your protection, it is a general question which I consider to be important. Do you have any permanent source of income?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just now, you mean? I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So your family is taken care of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relatively speaking, yes, considering my condition of health and the general circumstances I am living in, but generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, do you meet in premises or clubs together with former detainees, wherever you are now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean detainees from Celebici or other camps? I meet only with one person who was in Celebici, because he happens to be in the same town as me, and with other people, mostly people who spent two and more years in Zenica, because I have no other neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During those meetings, do you recount the horrors that you lived through in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes we do, sometimes we do not, it depends on what the subject of the conversation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What subjects do you talk about? What do they say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The people you have contact with who were former detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They talk about the conditions under which they lived, whether they were beaten, what the food was like, whether they had beds or did not have beds, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: After you left the camp, and when you reached where you are living now, did the authorities give you medical aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities did not, but I had to look for it myself, because of the disease that was developing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, to judge from your testimony, you suffered very heavy blows on your head, you had a broken rib; have you managed to have all that treated? Have you recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To some extent, yes, as far as my broken nose and my head. But I still have consequences due to my broken ribs and spinal injuries and very low blood pressure, and also I have problems with my spine that I referred to yesterday. I have had to see a chiropractor continuously because there are no other ways of fixing the vertebrae except manually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any medical reports to confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on me, I did not know that was necessary, but I could have brought the reports from two chiropractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are they private medical people with their own surgeries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, Mr. R, and also during the cross-examination by my learned colleague that preceded me, you said that you were questioned by the representative of the OTP office, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, when you were questioned by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, did they ask you any additional questions in addition to the statement you were making?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the statement I made or to any questions immediately prior to the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am not aware that you spoke to the investigators immediately before your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that two or three hours ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but I think the answers and questions are going too close to each other. I ask your Honour to remind the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I think we tell the witness he must wait for the translation, he has no idea how to do that, because he does not know where to hear the translation. It needs to be explained to him he can hear the translation through the other set of earphones. If they are on the right channel and turned up high enough, he will be able to hear when the English translation finishes. Without doing that, instructions to him to listen to the translation are not particularly useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I did not know, as you said, because I am only listening to one channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, when you were examined by the investigator of The Hague Tribunal, did the investigators ask you questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me make myself clear: you said everything that you considered important, and did they after that ask you additional questions about certain things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not interpreted).

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you said probably yes, do you recall what those questions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those could only have been questions to make my statement more precise. If I said there was a killing or a beating, then the question would be, "from what distance could you observe that? Did you personally eyewitness that? Did you personally hear that? How long did the beating last?" The questions were of that nature, there was no additional initiation of new subjects, it was merely to make my comments more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let us focus on that investigation. After the conversation was completed, did you receive a copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the gentleman who was taking the statement was in a hurry, so that I did not see a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you receive it subsequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, perhaps also because I changed my residence in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, you said you had a rifle, you described it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My question is: did you have that rifle before 13th April 1992, before the outbreak of the conflict in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not before 13th April, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you have that rifle in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got the rifle in the period between the first and second attack on Bradina, that is between 12th and 25th May, and of course it was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Where at home did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I explain? I have no idea, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was it hidden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was at home, of course it was hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It may not mean that, it may be readily visible to anyone who enters the house. I am asking you the question: was the rifle concealed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sense that it was not at the door or at the window, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the bedroom, shall we call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were there any other weapons in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was there any ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there were 20 or so bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, Mr. R, you said that Bradina was attacked by Croats and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Will you be so kind as to tell us how you know they were Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because from the direction of the west, from Repovci, were attacks by Croatian forces and most of the shelling came from that direction, because the Croats were far better armed than the Muslims were at that time, and the attacks from all the other sides came from the Muslims, because they were more numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But how do you know that Muslims came from one side and Croats from the other, as you have indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was pushed back from the railway station, or rather I retreated to the centre of town, when I saw this army or men in uniform coming in from Repovci and setting light to everything in front of them. The people who fled at that moment from that part, this hamlet which is known as Sunjina Strana, said that they were Croats and that they even recognised some of them. Also there was probably troops of the regular army of the Republic of Croatia, because they reached Konjic already in April, and were put up in the motel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? You said probably. Are you assuming or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard about those reports, I was still working in Konjic, and I heard that a Split company had come and was accommodated at the motel in Konjic and the people were terrified what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: A Split company, a company from Split, how did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the rumour in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you heard from others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You described during the examination-in-chief that at the moment of the attack on Bradina, you were digging your potato patch, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and let me add, I was captured in the rubber boots I was wearing in the garden and blue overalls and a sweater that I was wearing at the time. Rubber boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Where was your family at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family, when the attack started, when the shelling started, were in my apartment, but they later sought shelter in the infirmary in Bradina, or maybe even in the cellar of the cafe owned by Pero Mrkajic, I do not know because I had no contact with them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between the place you were arrested and that cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distance is about ten metres, but the cellar is one thing, the army another and the shooting something else. I could not enter the cellar myself. I saw my family for the last time on 25th May, and the next time I met up with them was in April 1994, that is almost a year later, when the Muslim-Croat conflicts started in the territory of the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, that actually means that you men, 18 of you, as you had said, were separated and the women and children were separate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you were taken prisoner, together with 17 of your comrades, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody in that group had some sort of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were different kinds of rifles from hunting rifles that some had, with permits, to semi-automatic rifles, maybe some even had automatic rifles, I do not know exactly what everybody had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, you said that during the attack on Bradina, 60 Serbs were killed, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is an approximate number, and let me elaborate. I was never a witness or was ever taken to identify the killed people in front of the church in Bradina or those who were then buried in a common grave there. However, there was a prisoner, his name is Veseljko Milanic, who was taken to Bradina to identify those massacred bodies in a church in Bradina and he said that maybe 40 to 45 people were put in that common grave and that new bodies were daily found in the woods and houses and they were being buried there or in other places. However, that common grave was so badly -- it was not covered properly so there were limbs that were sticking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, you showed a remarkable memory in certain aspects and you mentioned 60 people who were killed during the attack on Bradina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this information can be obtained from other people from Bradina. I only worked in Bradina, I was not from Bradina and I did not know many people there. However, I could name some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My question to you now is if you do not know which 60 Serbs these people were, do you assume or do you base that on what you were told by others or on your own experience? We have time, so take your time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said in what way I heard about this number. Also after my release from the prison, I met a number of women who were actually handling those bodies, whether they were their husbands or sons and were burying them. I could not have been a witness because I was already in Celebici at the time or on the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. R. However, based on your statements, it appears as your direct testimony, so this is what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statements that I had given earlier were not given as testimony like the one I am giving today, to give very precise information. This was more general statement on different occasions. If necessary, I could name a certain number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That would not be necessary. I understood what you said and it is satisfactory to me, thank you. Mr. R, during the examination-in-chief, when you were examined by my esteemed colleague Mr. Turone, you said that during your arrest in Bradina, you had to run a gauntlet to get on the truck, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were the soldiers on both sides of this gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were the soldiers lined up very densely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right one next to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were they all beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were they beating every prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, every prisoner who went through the gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How long was this cordon or gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, it could have been about 15 metres long, I already explained the position that we had to assume to pass through this cordon, we had to put our hands like this (indicates), we had to restrict our vision by our elbows and then the blows would follow on these exposed and unprotected areas which were very sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So densely lined up soldiers, 15 metres to the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that those were the exact measurements, that is approximate. Densely lined up soldiers, but whether it was 12, 15, 17 metres long, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But as you say, 12 or 15 or 17, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, when you gave your statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, why did you mention a 300 long cordon, whereas you said to the judge in Belgrade that it was 70 metres long, and now you are telling us today that it was 12 or 15 or 17, so you are saying 12 to 17 metres today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I am sure that I never said that it was 300 metres long, the cordon. If you have that, please show it to me. I am also convinced that in the statement in Belgrade, I also did not say that the cordon was 70 metres long, I would also like to see that part of the statement, if you have it on you. I said pretty much what I said today, so I never mentioned 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, you exclude the possibility that the cordon was in your different statements described as 300 metres, 70 metres long and 12, 15 or 17 metres and you say that the truth is what you said today, that is that it was 12, 15 or 17 metres long; do I have you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any event, I never said 300 metres, unless this was put into my statement later without my knowledge, and I abide by the statement that I have made today. I think that you do not have such a document where it states 300 metres, unless it was put in it later without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, on 2nd March 1994 -- before the investigating judge, so this is not a casual occasion -- before Judge Ilija Simic and pursuant to Article 141 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia stated that exactly, and you also signed every single page of the statement that you gave to the investigating judge and my colleague, the investigating judge in Belgrade, did forewarn you that you had to -- you were under an obligation to speak the truth, that you were not to omit anything and he also warned you of the consequences of perjury, and he also advised you that you did not have to answer certain questions and, as every practising judge, he said that you would be facing severe consequences of imprisonment should you be telling lies. So you signed this statement given to the Judge Simic and you signed not only once but you signed every single page, which was the usual practice and as is usual in all criminal systems in all of the issuing states in the area, you signed every single page of this record and in it it states that the cordon was 300 metres long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In no investigation or anywhere else did I say it was 300 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. R, when you were questioned by the investigators of the International Criminal Tribunal for War Crimes, you stated that this cordon was 70 metres long -- I apologise, you stated to the investigator 300 metres and to the investigating judge 70 metres. What I say to you now is based on the record of the statement that you yourself have given and signed. How is it possible that we have such a discrepancy? It is not the same thing that if you were beaten along the 300 metre long cordon or 12 to 15 metre long cordon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I know that I never said that this cordon was 300 metres long. I do not recall that I said that it was 70 metres long. I may have said 17. I do not know what was typed up and I do not know what you have in front of you, but I never said that the cordon was 300 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, I am going to show you the record of the interview that you gave on 2nd March 1994, and I would like to ask the usher's assistance to -- I am afraid we only have a Serbian version of it, there is no translation, so I would like the usher to please show you the record that you have signed. I also have an English translation, even though --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D8/2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I comment on this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Please do not comment on it, just review it with respect to what we have talked about, whether it states 300 metres long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It states: "As soon as we turned in the weapons, they brought in a truck with canvas" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not say that the cordon was 70 metres long, it says we had to cover 70 metres to get to the truck. 300 metres is never mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D9/2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please allow me to review the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that this is the document given to Mr. Regis?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. R.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already mentioned that because of a very short time during which the statement was given to Mr. Regis, it was never authorised. I never signed it and I never received any confirmation later on with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So what is stated there is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Three hundred metres is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Why would Mr. Abribat --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object to a question about why another person might have written something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I do not know, I am just asking, maybe he did tell him why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, do you claim that you did not sign the statement given to Mr. Abribat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that it was very pressing when I gave this statement and he said he was going to send it to me, but this is the first time I see it in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You have an excellent memory, could you please answer what you know. When you were giving the statement to Mr. Abribat, did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, I cannot answer that question, because I know that he kept putting off his flight a couple of times, he left the room to delay his flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would it not be on the statement itself if it was signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, he did sign, and the signature does exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then there is no need to ask a round about question. It either exists or it does not exist. I just mentioned the circumstances and the manner in which the statement was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, I am going to show you the statement you gave to the investigating judge in Belgrade and I am going to read you the whole paragraph from that statement, and this is what you said and I quote: "On 26th May 1992, Croatian troops, which was the Split company with the Muslim troops, surrounded Bradina and we had to surrender. Near the railway station, 18 of us surrendered because we were promised that nothing would happen to us. However, as soon as we surrendered our weapons, they brought a truck with covered" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly slow down your speed so that they can interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise: "... a canvas-covered truck and we had to pass the distance of about 70 metres to this truck through a cordon of soldiers who, as we were passing through, beat us." Did you say that to the investigating judge in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but an explanation here --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I just want you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot just say simply yes or no. First you said that you speak Croatian and I speak Serbian. In fact I speak Herzegovinan if you really want, and I did not say "doterati", but "dotjerati", which is Herzegovinan dialect and I think that the sentence can stand just as I put it. As soon as we surrendered the weapons, we had to cover a distance of 70 metres to the truck. That does not imply that the cordon was 70 metres long, that the distance was 70 metres long between where we put down our weapons and the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, however, since you say that the judge was putting in wrong words, it is not your speech, does that mean that the judge also made factual errors in what he was putting down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if the word "doterati" and "dotjerati" mean the same thing or not, I do not know if that is a right assumption or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did the investigating judge wrongly write down this 70 metres that you had to cover? Did he misunderstand you or you just simply did not say that and he wrote it down?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, it is asked and answered. He already explained that the distance was 70 metres, but that did not meant that even the gauntlet should be 70 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I thank you, my learned colleague Turone, in this way, but that is not the question that I asked. My question was whether the judge misunderstood the witness or just simply wrongly put down what the witness told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, he cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which do you think is more consistent with the facts? You can see from the explanation what is more realistic. Why do you push the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I do not insist on it, I just wanted additional clarification, but I am satisfied with the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, is it true that when you were driven from Bradina to Celebici that you were beaten on the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were all the detainees beaten in the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all of them, because we were crammed in, depending on who jumped first, so that those people who were further forward were not beaten, only those who came last were beaten. I remember that in the case of Simo Mrkajic, a guard kicked him in the jaw and that his teeth were knocked out. The teeth were on the floor of the truck. So that everyone was not beaten, the beating continued so people tried to escape it by moving further forward, so that those who were right next to the driver's cabin probably were not beaten. So the position that we held was that we had our hands behind our heads, that no names were to be used, that we had to look down, I have already described this several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It emerged from your examination-in-chief that you were more or less all of you very severely beaten upon your capture and while being driven to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the gauntlet and also in the truck, as I have already said, those who were closer to the driver got less, those behind got more. It is very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, Mr. R, that the subsequent prisoners who were brought to Celebici were also beaten upon detention or immediately upon arriving in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because our truck was the first to reach the Celebici camp and the tunnel, and after they had done with us, other trucks and other prisoners arrived and all of them were beaten in the same way and thrown into the tunnel in the same way. I also know that in the case of some people like Dr. Relja Mrkajic, his glasses were intentionally broken so that he could not see. That is just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, during the examination-in-chief, you said that Mr. Zdravko Mucic was never present when somebody was beaten as far as you saw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was never present when someone was beaten? I said very clearly and precisely that I saw Mr. Zdravko Mucic, Pavo, for the first time when I left tunnel number 9, that he came to hangar number 6 twice and I also can assert that I personally was not present when somebody was being beaten and Mr. Mucic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. R, as an exemplary soldier, a squad leader who was awarded during your military service, do you know that according to the constitution of the former state, who is entitled to sign a surrender? Did anyone have that authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody, probably Tito did because he was omnipotent in his day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the death penalty was envisaged for capitulation if anyone were to sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Then according to that law, how should somebody behave when he finds himself in enemy captivity? May he co-operate with the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that question a little? What do you mean by not being allowed to co-operate with the enemy and the right to capitulation? I do not understand the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. Is it the duty of a loyal citizen of SFRY, the former state, when in captivity to do everything he can to escape, according to the laws that were valid in the former state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But no one respected the laws at that point in time, that had no relevance at the time at all. Secondly, since our families were also detained at the school in Bradina, any attempt to escape or to do anything would certainly have terrible reprisals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, tell me, why did you not tell The Hague investigators that when you were arrested in Bradina, you had a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday already that I did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the examination-in-chief, when my learned colleague Turone asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am here under oath and I am telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that is the reason, the reason that you were not under oath, that you did not tell the investigator the same thing when he examined you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. (Pause). Does it say anywhere in this statement that I said that I did not have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, it does not, but no mention of a rifle is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I was not asked about that, I was asked how I was captured, here it does not say anywhere I did have a rifle or I did not have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, but when you were making that statement with the investigating judge in Belgrade, you said that you had a rifle -- just a moment, please. Let us just wait for the interpretation. And now, or rather when examined by the investigator, you did not mention the rifle, so my question now is: did the investigators ask you additionally whether you were armed when you were captured, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, I am referring to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They never put that question to me, I was just asked to explain where and how I was captured. As for the statement itself, the statement as it stands was more detailed than this, but because of the shortness of time and the translation, probably that is the reason why it appears in a shorter version, so anyway, no one asked me whether I was armed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sir, at your first examination, and I am referring to the statement you made for the investigating judge in Belgrade, why did you not say that while you were being transported from Bradina to Celebici in a truck that you were beaten with metal poles, to explain, whereas when speaking to the investigator of the International Tribunal, you did refer to metal poles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said early on today that these statements were given on different occasions, and I hope that you too appreciate that, that two statements can never be identical. One statement contains a certain set of details, another, because if I were able to repeat the same statement, I would be a robot or a computer, but I still hope I am a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you do not know why you did not mention the metal poles during the first examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said that, but the statement was probably shortened for various reasons. But now here we are, we have the opportunity to make any corrections if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your first examination by the investigating magistrate in Belgrade, why did you say on that occasion that several of your ribs were broken and later on, when you were examined by The Hague investigator, you said that only one rib had been broken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to whether it was one or several ribs, even now, if anyone wants to see and feel with their fingers, they may do so. I know that one rib is broken and several others were cracked, so there is a slight imprecision in the wording that you are now pinpointing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question? Why did you say at the first investigation several ribs and then only one rib when speaking to The Hague investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I withdraw that question, thank you. When you were speaking to the investigating magistrate in Belgrade, why did you not tell that magistrate the way in which Zdravko Mucic lined you up in front of the guards and what he told you about greater Serbia as you told us here during the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because no one asked me about that. Here the emphasis was on individual instances of death, beatings and torture, and probably at that moment the judge did not consider it important, so he did not put it down in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. R, have you read Dante?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean, "you who enter leave all hope behind"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is going to take us a few minutes because of the electrical problems here. Would the court like to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have difficulties of your continuing immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There is no problem, your Honour, just whatever pleases the court pleases me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would just like to remind the court that my audio output is dead and that was what Mr. Moran was implying. I normally split with him. Maybe I can move to his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that may be the appropriate way to solve our electrical problem, while I get wired. (Pause). May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and I am going to be asking you some questions. I would like to see if we can set a few ground rules before I start. The first thing is sometimes the questions I ask frankly are not as precise as they ought to be, and if I ask you a question that confuses you, that you do not understand, will you stop me and I will work with you if it takes all day so you understand it, fair enough? That was the next thing I was going to ask you. You just nodded your head. You will see there are two ladies over here with funny machines, one in front of you, and one over there. They are stenographers and they have to take down every word we say and they cannot take down a nod. Instead of nodding yes or no like we would in a conversation, if you would say yes or no, I would appreciate that and I think they would also. Can you do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One other thing, and I think it will get us done quicker and get us all out of here and you home quicker, if you will listen to the question I ask and just answer the question I ask, I think we can all be done with this in as painless a way as possible; fair enough, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is not what a nod means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Let us start off, I will not try any surprises on you, I will tell you when I am going to change subjects, so there is no confusion to anybody. You were born in the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Except for your years in Konjic you have essentially lived in Konjic municipality your entire life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the municipality of Konjic up to the completion of elementary school, I completed my secondary school in Mostar and the university in Sarajevo. After that, I lived within the territory of the municipality of Konjic, where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You are a person from Konjic, basically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Back, what, in March 1992, there was a referendum in Bosnia on independence, you recall that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a referendum, but I do not know any details about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, sir, the only question I am going to ask is this -- I do not care if you voted or, if you did vote, how you voted, because that is your business, it is none of my business. All I want to know is, if you had desired to vote, could you have voted in that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you a definitive answer, possibly I could have, but I really do not know when it was held, exactly where, and I did not participate. Probably I could have if I had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the answer, I think. That is the answer you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He gave me exactly the answer and I want to thank him for that. Another thing, let us jump ahead to the defence of Bradina. We are both old artillery men and you know what a chain of command is, in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There was no military organisation in Bradina with a chain of command, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There were no commanders or subcommanders or anything like that, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can say is that there were some kind of commanders. My immediate commander was Vaso Vujicic, I got the rifle from him and the orders to go towards the railway station when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall you testified earlier, none of you had any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were not wearing kind of badges or insignia or arm bands, or anything to identify yourself as part of the defence force, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I already explained what my clothes were, what I was wearing rather when I was captured and how I was taken to Celebici, in rubber boots, blue overalls and a green sweater.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Really you were not even taking part in the defence when you were captured, you were just digging your potatoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said at the moment Bradina was attacked, I was in my garden digging potatoes, that Vaso Vujicic ran up and said that Bradina had been attacked from all sides and that I should go towards the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fair. My memory was not as good as yours. Let us talk about memories for a second, let us change subjects again. Sometimes I have a hard time remembering what I had for lunch yesterday and I am sure you may very well be the same way. The further back in time an event is, the less well I remember the details. I think we all agree that is true for most people; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happens to everyone. As far as your memory is concerned, it must be better than mine, because your legal training gives you this greater ability to remember details, but as you say, it is the normal human process of forgetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Oh but it was true that my memory was that good, sir. I think you talked to Mr. Ackerman about those three statements that you made, the one to the Serbian Counsel Information Centre back in 1993 at some point, and then the interview you gave in the District Court of Belgrade in March 1994, and finally the statement that you gave to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor back in October 1995. As I recall your testimony, stop me if I am wrong, it is that when you were giving those statements you were giving them to the best of your memory, answering questions as truthfully as you could; if somebody did not ask a question you did not answer it, but it reflects the best memory that you had at that time; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. It can be said like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Last week when you were meeting with Mr. Turone, you had a chance at least to quickly review those statements, all three of them, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have already said how it happened. I asked Mr. Turone whether I could carefully read those statements, and he answered the way I have already said, he said, "all you have in your memory is sufficient, there is no need for any additional reading". I asked for a careful review.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That might have refreshed your memory, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I can understand that those kinds of things could occur, that that would help refresh your memory. I understand that sometimes there is going to be details in these statements that are not there, your testimony may be lacking in details; for instance, what was it Mr. Abribat did not ask you, if you had a weapon; do you recall testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the interpretation is not quite correct. Could you please give me a sentence that I can answer with yes or no as regards Mr. Abribat?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. Your statement to Mr. Abribat does not mention one way or the other whether you had a weapon in Bradina and as I recall your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No mention is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall your testimony, the reason that that is not there is because he never asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So that is an example of what I am talking about, that sometimes the details between the statements will be different, but basically --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But basically each one of the statements reflected the best memory you had about what you were talking about at the time you made the statement; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good. That is what I have been dancing around to get. I may not have been as artful about it as I could have been, but I appreciate you struggling through this with me. The day you were captured was what, January 26th 1992 or was it the 25th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: January?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May, I am sorry, May 25th 1992. Was that not the day you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 26th May in the evening. I know it was the evening. I think it was 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, and you were taken immediately to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that truck went directly to the Celebici camp. The one in front of us went to Musala for beatings. Our truck did not visit Konjic, it drove directly to Celebici and then what happened was what I have been telling you about this past two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. The first day you were there, which would have been the 25th or 26th May, the first day you were there was the day that there were these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall, you testified that a man named Hazim Delic was there at those beatings, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the night of the beatings, I did not indicate who was there on the first night of the beatings because I described the position, manner the whole procedure, but somebody from the immediate vicinity issued the commands, saying, "that is enough".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether that was Hazim Delic? One way or the other. If you do not know, you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I did not even mention him in that context, I did mention him in other contexts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. After those beatings, you were all stripped to your underwear and put into tunnel number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You were locked in tunnel number 9 for some period of time, about a week, and during that period --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And during that period, the only water you got was, what, this industrial water you talked about, it was pretty filthy stuff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the first day we got the proper drinking water from the command building and later that stopped. In number 6, even that kind of poor quality water was reduced to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My notes from yesterday indicate that the time you were in tunnel 9 and you were getting this industrial water, it was so filthy that there were pieces of faeces in it; do you recall testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, and that is the truth. I also said that for a long time after leaving the camp, I had problems with my liver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I thought we would have a deal you would listen to my question and answer it. Like I say, that will get us out of here a little quicker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, thank you. You also as I recall testified that there was urine and excrement all over tunnel 9 and the level of that stuff started rising in the tunnel because the tunnel sloped downward; do you remember testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know what the exact precise statement you are referring to, the tunnel was sloping downwards and this last part was flat, so that as it filled up with urine and faeces, the level rose and flooded part of the tunnel where we were lying, so it was occupying more space so that there was less left for us to sit and lie on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There were about 70 people jammed in there that week, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said on the first night, I think I said 77 on the first night, but the number varied immediately during that first week. Some were transferred to number 6, I mentioned just my own case when I was transferred, I know that some people were directly moved from there to the sports hall in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How many people that were in there came down with cholera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that anyone got cholera, but I know that everyone had a diarrhoea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, I think we will take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I take two more minutes and then that will be a perfect time to break, a change of subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did many people get typhus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that anyone contracted typhus. All I know, I repeat, was terrible cases of diarrhoea and loss of body weight. I weighed about 88 kilograms when I was captured and when I left, I weighed 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So no one had typhus, no one had cholera. Your Honour, I think this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: A break for a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Only a break, not a conclusion, but I thank your Honour's indulgence for letting me finish off the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break now and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about set to mention a name and I would like to mention it in private session, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we go into closed session now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, we are back in public session, and everyone out in the audience can hear us, if they are there. Remember on direct you testified about a couple of days after you were thrown into tunnel number 9 and some guards came in and passed a helmet and told you to put all of your valuables in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That name I mentioned, that man, was he one of the people that did that? If you do not know, you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it was at night and at the beginning, I did not know the majority of people in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know that man whose name I mentioned in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him personally, but I know that he was in Celebici at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You do not recall whether he was one of the people that passed the helmet or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall. In fact, nobody did pass it around, the helmet was passed in at the entrance and then people were passing it on among themselves to put things inside. Nobody walked inside. The practice was for the guards not to enter during the night. Maybe Mr. Delic did come in, but only much later in August. He would come into number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let us change subjects again. Let me follow something up you just said, but it does not have to do with that man. Did I understand your testimony was that it was a rare occasion for a guard to go either into tunnel 9 or hangar 6 at night until August? Did I understand you to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think again we agree that it was a rare thing for that to happen at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the way until August, until Mr. Delic came in several times. Up until then, the guards would call out from the doorstep, they would call the prisoners out by their names and then bring them out, beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine. Sir, let us change subjects again for a second, okay? You testified yesterday about the death of Miroslav Vujcic, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I recall your testimony, you testified that Mr. Delic had been involved in that shooting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was in the tunnel at that time and that we only heard beatings and cries, and later, excuse me, after the burst of fire, you could hear the voice, "he fled, God damn it" and then we saw his brother Radoslav and he said, "Delic killed Miroslav".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So the source of your information that it was Mr. Delic who killed him was Mr. Vujcic's brother Radoslav, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You have absolutely no personal knowledge one way or the other except what Radoslav Vujcic told you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This personal experience, partial or whatever, is such that we could hear the voice of Miroslav, in fact I heard Miroslav's voice, because I knew him for at least ten years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but the question I had for you was that the source of your information for Mr. Delic's involvement in this shooting is Radoslav Vujcic; that is what you testified to today and that is what you testified to yesterday, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the help of the usher? Here are copies for the court, the Registry and one for the Prosecutor. Your Honour, I move to introduce under whatever the next number is a portion of Radoslav Vujcic's statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. So I could narrow it down, it is the cover page that has a Bates number of 00385415, the signature page, which has a Bates number of 00385419, and one paragraph of the first page, which has a Bates number of 00385416. That paragraph starts as the fifth paragraph from the top, starts off "when we arrived in Celebici"; specifically, your Honour, I am introducing it for the limited purpose of impeaching the declarant to that statement, which would be Mr. Radoslav Vujcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is the declarant here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness testified that the declarant for the statement that Mr. Delic was involved in the shooting was Radoslav Vujicic. This is Mr. Vujcic's statement about that. Like I say, I am just limiting the offer. I have given the court and the Registry clean copies, but all I am offering is the front page, the signature page and the one paragraph that I identified, which is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is the number of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The first page says "witness statement" at the top, the last number, the Bates number at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The fifth paragraph, starts off "when we arrived in Celebici".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He states he does not know who killed his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Like I say, it is not to impeach this witness, it is to impeach Mr. Vujcic's statement to this witness, that is what the offer is for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can impeach him only with reference to his statement. How can you impeach him with reference to someone else's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not impeaching this witness. I am not saying that Mr. Vujcic did not tell him that. My position is that what he told Mr. R is different from what he said to the Prosecutor, so the declarant, Mr. Vujcic, is impeached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe Radoslav made a false statement to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is possible, your Honour, that is my position, it is conceivably possible. I am not impugning this man at all. If the court would like, I can deliver another copy of this statement that has everything else blacked out and just including the one paragraph of the offer, plus the front page and the signature page; whatever makes the court happy makes me happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not a question of happiness here. We are talking about irregularities, not about happiness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you producing Radoslav as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We are not calling Radoslav Vujicic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Greaves just pointed out to me that this goes to the trustworthiness under Tadic of the statement from Radoslav Vujicic to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I agree, but how does it get in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it gets in to (i) show the untrustworthiness of the statement given by Mr. Vujicic to this witness here, and (ii) it shows that the person who actually made the statement that is in front of the court, that Mr. Delic was involved in the shooting, has made two different statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It will not be sufficient to say that the witness was not told something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am not saying the witness -- my position is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Even if you look at the dates when he told him this, gave him this information, it was much earlier than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me clear that up with one quick question, your Honour. Sir, when Mr. Vujcic, Radoslav, gave you this information about his brother's death, that was while you were in the camp, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, immediately upon entering the hangar 6. Radoslav was in very bad shape, his hands were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, that is fine, thank you. Your Honour, again, the statement that Radoslav made ... Judge Jan, your microphone is on and I can hear you fairly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As a judge, I do not talk about some thing which I do not want other people to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I promised Mr. Hocking some months ago that if this occurred I would warn you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is in open court, it does not matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it a potentially exculpatory matter should be filed in these proceedings? I do not see how you can, through this witness, who was told a thing on the day it happened, which is usually the best evidence there is, but on this, which is considerably later -- but for such a serious matter to have escaped -- as I was saying, it was long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have just been informed first by Mr. Greaves -- and I know the Tribunal is not bound by the national rules of evidence and I am not asking you to adopt them, but Mr. Greaves has told me that he has seen, in the United Kingdom, cases where what we would call hearsay -- one time, he says -- what we would call hearsay, where an inconsistent prior statement by the declarant was admitted, and I can tell you that under the American Federal Rules of Evidence, specifically I think it is Rule 805 -- is that correct? It is either 805 or 806. It is specifically provided for in the American national rules, and I think the reason for it is this: if a Tribunal of any type is going to consider statements made by other people out of court, you have to be able to look at the reliability of that statement. An example that comes to mind is out of Judge Cassese's book with Judge Roling on the Tokyo Tribunal, where a statement on Foreign Minister Ribbentrop in Germany that he made just a few days before he was executed came in and the way Judge Roling, who was the judge on the Tokyo Tribunal, analysed it was there was two things you had to look at: one, did Mr. Ribbentrop make this statement, and I am not disputing the fact that Radoslav Vujicic made the statement to this witness, and then the second thing the court should look at is, is the statement true. His own statement goes to the truth of that, it goes to the weight this court ought to give what Mr. Vujicic told this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How does it become a part of the proceedings, this is what I am trying --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it comes in for the very limited purpose, not of substantive evidence, not to show that Mr. Delic did or did not do anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But to show that there is an inconsistent statement about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the person who has made the statement that has been introduced to the Tribunal, that is correct, your Honour, and that is all I am offering it for. Again, it does not go to show whether Mr. Vujicic made the statement, but whether what he told this person is a true fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see your point, I agree, there are two statements which are inconsistent about the same matter, credited to the same person. How do we get his second statement into evidence, that is what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I try to shed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not part of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And it is not reliable, that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it goes to the weight the court ought to give the hearsay evidence that was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, you exclude that, saying it was not reliable, because the evidence is only admissible if it is reliable and has probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not want to sound like Mr. Niemann on this, but we have trained judges here and it helps me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you reject one, you must have the two to compare. How do we get this into evidence? That is the point. I suppose Mr. Ackerman is anxious to assist, so let us hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not know if I can be of any assistance at all, but it seems to me that in a situation where the Trial Chamber, based upon the Tadic decision, on occasion lets in evidence that would be excluded as hearsay where I come from, for instance, what is always at issue then is the reliability of that out of court statement. Did that out of court statement that you have heard, in this case what Radoslav Vujicic said to this witness, is that a reliable statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is made, that is the second point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it reliable, because if it is not reliable it should not come in. It seems to me there are two possibilities. Number one, this court could say, based upon the document presented to it, it can now retroactively determine that that statement was not reliable and exclude it from the evidence and exclude it from your consideration; or secondly, you can go ahead and admit this document as evidence of the reliability of the statement that has been admitted and consider the weight that it might have in showing that and therefore in your deliberations weigh the reliability of the statement that has been admitted through this witness. There are two ways to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The first consideration I have pointed out has still not been answered, how do we get it into the proceedings, because it is exculpatory and should be in the proceedings. You cannot get it into proceedings through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a statement which shows on its face that it was taken by the Office of the Prosecutor and was provided to us in discovery, and I do not think that anyone from over there will dispute that that is in fact what occurred. I have no reason to believe that that statement is anything other than what it purports to be, a statement taken by an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor on February 21st 1996, properly interpreted by the -- just the way every other statement is. So the authentication, unless the Prosecution wants to take the position, and I do not think they will, that it is not what it purports to be, in fact I bet they are willing to stipulate that it is what it purports to be, that it is a document provided to us in discovery that is a statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course it was a statement provided to the Defence lawyers by the Prosecution, your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no dispute about the genuineness of this statement, because it was recorded by your office. There are two ways open: we have it tendered in before us or strike off that portion in which he refers to how the death of this particular person occurred as unreliable hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have no objection to the tendering of this document, your Honour, provided this is done not to impeach this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (inaudible) that person would be telling a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pardon me, your Honour, it is admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I said we can take it into evidence as an admitted document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, I am just offering the one paragraph plus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It does not matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us follow your background for tendering it. You lay the foundation for tendering it by asking the question, then you point out to him that this is the statement from this gentleman, it states to the contrary, then you can put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, did someone deliver a copy of that statement to you, Mr. R? You said that you read some English; is your English good enough to read that document? I notice you were flipping through it, especially that one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sure he can. He has read Dante's "Inferno".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he has read Dante's Inferno, he has read a lot more than I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He quoted a passage from the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Dante is in Italian, but I shall do my best to read this too. The sentence roughly says that soldiers cried out, "a Chetnik has escaped", and that a soldier shot at him. When he fell, another soldier shot him in the back, or the back of his head, with three bullets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
